analysis.one_liner: Requires large employers to provide and help pay for comprehensive family health insurance for their workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to five House committees and died in committee when the 108th Congress ended, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal wage-and-hour law to require any employer with 50 or more employees to offer each worker a family health plan as comprehensive as the Blue Cross Blue Shield plan offered to federal employees, and to pay at least the same share of the premium the federal government pays for federal workers — roughly seven of every ten dollars. Workers would pay their share through payroll deduction, and coverage would have to start within 30 days of being hired. Contract workers would count as employees, so firms could not dodge the requirement by using contractors. Employers who failed to comply would face federal penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees of firms with 50 or more workers — including contract workers — and their spouses and children would gain guaranteed access to comprehensive family health coverage, with the employer picking up most of the premium and coverage starting within 30 days of hire. The bill's own findings note that about 40 million Americans were uninsured and that most of them were workers or their dependents.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at large employers and their families

how_it_helps.text: It requires every large employer — one with 50 or more employees, including contract workers — to offer each employee a health plan covering the employee and family, with benefits at least as good as the Blue Cross Blue Shield Standard Plan offered to federal employees.

Employers must pay at least the same share of the premium the federal government pays for that federal employee plan (roughly seven of every ten dollars), with reduced contributions for part-time workers.
Coverage must begin within 30 days of starting a job, and the bill counts contract workers as employees, so firms cannot avoid the obligation by staffing themselves with contractors.
Enforcement includes civil money penalties against employers who do not comply, modeled on existing pension-law enforcement, and states may layer stricter requirements on top.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 50 or more employees would bear most of the premium cost for every employee, including contract workers. Workers would pay their share through payroll withholding. Employees on Medicare, Medicaid, or other federal health programs would generally have to switch to their employer's plan or have that program pay their premium share.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a new, substantial cost for employers with 50 or more employees, who would have to pay most of the premium for every employee, including contract workers. Businesses could absorb that through slower hiring, lower wages, or higher prices — costs that fall partly on workers themselves.
The bill only helps workers at large employers. The unemployed, and employees of small firms below the 50-employee threshold, get nothing; the vast majority of the uninsured would not all be reached.

Employees enrolled in Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, or CHAMPUS would generally be required to take their employer's offer instead, or have the federal program pay their premium share — a provision that shifts coverage (and potentially costs) between public programs and employer plans with unclear net effect for beneficiaries and taxpayers.

The required benefit level is pegged to the Blue Cross Blue Shield Standard Plan as it existed on January 1, 2004, so the adequacy of coverage would depend on a fixed benchmark rather than an updated standard over time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been large and concrete: guaranteed family coverage at FEHBP-quality levels for employees at firms with 50 or more workers, with employers picking up most of the premium, directly attacking the fact that most uninsured Americans are workers or their dependents. The costs are real and the bill's opponents would have pressed them hard: a new multibillion-dollar annual obligation on mid-size and large employers, some risk of slower hiring or lower cash wages, no help for workers at small firms or for the jobless, and possible added federal expense where employed Medicaid or Medicare beneficiaries chose to stay on public coverage. An honest accounting is that the bill tackled a genuine gap through the blunt instrument of an employer mandate rather than broader public coverage, and it was never amended, debated, or scored, so its real-world trade-offs were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to five House committees and several subcommittees, none of which ever voted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on September 16, 2003.
It was referred that day to five House committees: Education and the Workforce, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform, and Armed Services.

In late September and early October 2003 it was routed to subcommittees on Health, Total Force, Employer-Employee Relations, Workforce Protections, and Civil Service and Agency Organization, and the Defense Department was asked for comments — but no committee or subcommittee ever held a vote on it.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill expired without any floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers are better off: they never had to begin paying most of the cost of family health coverage for their employees, including contract workers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers who avoided new premium costs

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; no other member cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls were ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, and no member is on record in the provided sources as opposing it.

industries.note: The bill makes private employer-sponsored insurance the mandatory channel for covering millions of workers: every large employer must buy a qualifying private plan and insurers must comply with the new rules. Insurers gain a huge base of mandated customers whose premiums are mostly paid by employers and workers.

industries.industry: Large employers (50 or more employees, including those using contract labor)
industries.note: These firms would bear most of the premium cost for coverage for every employee, including contract workers, who the bill explicitly counts as employees. That is a direct new payroll expense, which businesses would otherwise keep or spend elsewhere.

industries.industry: Federal health programs (Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, CHAMPUS)
industries.note: Employees covered by these programs would generally have to take their employer's offer instead, moving working beneficiaries off public rolls. But on request the federal program must pay the employee's premium share, so the programs could still pick up part of the cost for some members.
